fuller.text: This encyclopedia article covers the dodo, an extinct bird that could not fly and lived only on Mauritius, an island east of Madagascar. It belonged to the pigeon and dove family, and its closest living relative is the Nicobar pigeon. The article covers its family tree, body, behaviour, extinction, surviving remains and place in culture.

fuller.text: The dodo died out less than a century after sailors first recorded it in 1598. According to the article, this drew attention to a problem not seen before: humans could cause whole species to disappear. It has since been called an "icon of extinction", partly through its role in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland.

fuller.text: Evidence is thin, because no complete specimen exists. Its looks come from 17th-century drawings, paintings and written accounts, which often disagree with each other. Many European paintings probably showed overfed captive birds or badly stuffed ones, making the dodo look fatter than it was. Most bones come from the Mare aux Songes swamp, which yielded remains of over 300 dodos but very few skulls or wing bones.

fuller.text: In 2002, researchers compared DNA from the Oxford specimen's foot with DNA from its extinct cousin, the Rodrigues solitaire. This confirmed both belonged in the pigeon family, with the Nicobar pigeon as their nearest living relative. The article warns that the DNA was degraded and none has come from bones, so these results still need checking. The two lines split about 23 million years ago, yet the islands are under 10 million years old, so the ancestors probably still flew. With no plant-eating mammals competing for food, both birds grew large and lost flight.

fuller.text: Studies of bones and old accounts suggest several things about the living bird. It stood about 62.6–75 cm tall, and wild weight estimates range from 10.6 to 17.5 kg, though weight is still debated. Leg bone strength suggests it could run quite fast, and its small wings may have served for display and balance. A 2016 brain cast showed a brain-to-body ratio like modern pigeons, so it was probably about as intelligent, despite its reputation.

fuller.text: Hunting by people was not the main cause of extinction, contrary to popular belief. Fewer than 50 people lived there in the 17th century, but they brought pigs, macaques, rats, dogs and cats, which raided nests and competed for food. Humans also cleared the forest the dodos lived in. One 2020 proposal blames wild pigs while the island was briefly unsettled, between 1658 and 1664.

fuller.text: The last widely accepted sighting was in 1662, but the exact date is disputed. A 2003 statistical study of later hunting records estimated 1693, likely somewhere between 1688 and 1715. Others argue later "dodo" reports really described the red rail, another flightless bird; the IUCN Red List accepts 1662.

fuller.text: The article's main conclusion is that the dodo was probably extinct by 1700, about a century after discovery. Long shown as fat and clumsy, it is now thought to have been well adapted to its home, though its exact appearance remains unresolved.

brief.text: This encyclopedia article is about the dodo, a big bird that could not fly. It lived only on Mauritius, an island in the Indian Ocean, and is now extinct. Its closest living relative is the Nicobar pigeon, so the dodo was really a giant pigeon.

Its closest living relative is the Nicobar pigeon, so the dodo was really a giant pigeon.

brief.text: Dutch sailors first wrote about the dodo in 1598, and the last widely accepted sighting was in 1662. The article says its quick loss first made people see that humans could wipe out a whole species. Hunting was not the main cause, though. Animals people brought, like pigs and monkeys, raided nests and ate its food, while forests were cut down.

brief.text: Old pictures show a fat, clumsy bird, but many were drawn from overfed or badly stuffed birds. Experts now think the dodo was well suited to its home and probably about as smart as pigeons.
